deep.reconstruction:
Setting (continued from p.17). A finite family of (pseudo-)hyperplanes H_i (i in I) cuts a sphere S. Each point x has a sign vector k(x) in E = prod_i D_{H_i}, where D_{H_i} = {0, +, -} is the 'V' poset 0 < + and 0 < -. E carries the product order. Sigma, a subset of E, is the set of realised sign vectors (in oriented-matroid language, the covectors without 0). Z*_alpha is the face with sign vector alpha. Sigma is given the Alexandrov ('infimum') topology, whose closed sets are the lower sets. P.17 showed that the closure of Z*_alpha is Z*_{closure of {alpha}}, the union of the faces Z*_beta with beta <= alpha.

This page.
(1) For any A in Sigma, the closure of Z*_A equals Z*_{closure of A}. Since A is finite, the closure of the union is the union of the closures. Then the union over alpha in A of closure{alpha} is the closure of A, because a finite union of lower sets is the lower set generated by A.
(2) Conclusion: the finite poset Sigma is the index poset of a stratification of S. The strata are nonempty, and the frontier/density axiom holds: the closure of Z*_alpha is Z_alpha, the union of the strata below alpha. The strata are connected. In modern terms, S is a stratified space whose strata poset is Sigma, and k: S -> Sigma is continuous for the Alexandrov topology.
(3) A crossed-out passage and a marginal drawing (marked '?') discuss whether Sigma is an 'I-ens' (apparently an inf-set: a poset in which bounded-below pairs have infima, or closed faces meet in closed faces). Counterexample: n >= 2 planes through a common line, e.g. n = 2. On S^2 this gives two great circles meeting at two antipodal vertices; this is the drawn digon picture. Two arcs of the same circle have closures meeting in two points, not in one closed face. Adjoining {0}, i.e. passing to the cone in R^{d+1}, repairs this: intersections of closed facets become closed facets.
(4) Claim: Sigma is an open part of E, i.e. upward closed: alpha in Sigma, beta in E, beta >= alpha implies beta in Sigma. Hence any lower ('minorante') subset of Sigma would be an I-ens, since meets in E are coordinatewise. A marginal note says '(cas idéal on a (Pi_3))', which seems to tie this to a genericity axiom (Pi_3).

Purpose: to encode a pseudo-line or pseudo-hyperplane system combinatorially as a finite poset / finite topological space whose stratified realisation recovers the sphere.
errors: The claim 'Sigma is an open (upward-closed) part of E' is false in general.

Counterexample for the openness claim: three great circles through a common pair of antipodal points on S^2 (three planes through a line). At a common vertex alpha = (0,0,0) we have beta = (+,-,-) >= alpha (with H_3 = {x - y = 0}), yet beta is not realised.

Openness holds exactly when the arrangement is locally simple: at each face, the hyperplanes containing it are independent. Presumably this is the 'cas idéal' (Pi_3); if not stated as a hypothesis, the claim is a gap. The crossed-out counterexample of n >= 2 planes through one line shows Grothendieck was aware of non-generic behaviour.

Even where Sigma is open, Sigma itself is not a lower set of E. The meet of two covectors in E (coordinatewise) need not lie in Sigma, e.g. the meet of opposite faces is 0, which is not in Sigma on the sphere. So 'I-ens' statements must be restricted to lower subsets, as he does.

ideas.what: Sign-vector map k: S -> E = prod{0,+,-} with order 0 < ±; faces = fibres; closure of a face = union of faces with smaller sign vector
ideas.modern_name: covectors / big face poset of an oriented matroid; topological representation of pseudo-arrangements

ideas.what: Viewing the face poset as a finite topological space (closed = lower sets) and the arrangement as a stratification indexed by it, with frontier axiom and connected strata
ideas.modern_name: Alexandrov topology; poset-stratified spaces; the face map S -> Sigma is continuous
ideas.usually_credited_to: Alexandrov (1937), McCord (1966); stratified-space formalism (e.g. Lurie, Higher Algebra appendix)
ideas.where_published: Spirit of 'tame topology' in Esquisse d'un programme (1984), not this specific statement

ideas.what: Closed faces need not meet in a closed face on the sphere (two great circles); adjoining the origin (cone) restores the meet property
ideas.modern_name: the face poset of a central arrangement with 0 adjoined is a meet-semilattice (lattice once a top is added)
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard oriented matroid theory (Björner et al. 1993, ch. 4)

ideas.what: Covector set is upward closed in E under a genericity hypothesis (Pi_3)
ideas.modern_name: simple / uniform arrangements: local completeness of sign patterns

deep.surprise_reason: This is an independent, careful rediscovery of the basic face-poset and stratification picture of (pseudo-)hyperplane arrangements in Grothendieck's finite-topology language. All of it is standard oriented-matroid material, and one claim (openness of Sigma) needs a genericity hypothesis. It is historically interesting as evidence of his 1981+ work on pseudo-line systems, but it contains nothing new.
transcription_corrections: The parenthetical formula should read: closure of the union over alpha in A of Z*_alpha equals the union over alpha in A of Z*_{closure of {alpha}}, which equals Z*_{union over alpha in A of closure{alpha}}, with an underbrace marking the last index as closure(A). The middle index is the closure of {alpha}, not {alpha}, and the stars are present.

In the second line the definition of the stratification ends 'satisfaisant à l'axiome de frontière (les Z*_alpha non vides, et de densité: closure of Z*_alpha = Z_alpha), et à strates connexes'. The insertion 'et de densité' sits on the left margin before the struck text.

The drawing in the left margin (marked '?') shows a sphere cut by two great circles meeting at two antipodal points, i.e. the case n = 2 planes through a common line. It illustrates the crossed-out counterexample.
The last lines are probably: 'Donc dans Sigma (et partie majorante [ouverte] commune dans E) toute partie minorante (cas idéal: on a (Pi_3)) ... toute partie minorante de Sigma = un I-ens'.
